topic.title: Ray diagrams for converging lenses: camera, projector and magnifying glass
topic.subject: science
topic.examWeightHint: The hardest topic in P2 by our own scoring, and it has appeared in every paper read for this batch. Summer 2024 Higher Q6(a) gave [5] for the magnifying-glass construction and [1] for naming the device; Summer 2025 Foundation Q3(b) and Higher Q7(b) both gave the construction and the image description together. Lenses are separate-Physics content on AQA and Edexcel, so almost every revision resource she will find outside this platform is labelled Triple.
mustMemorise: Axis, lens, F and 2F on both sides, object: the scaffolding comes first
Parallel in, through the far-side F out
Through the optical centre, straight on
Through the near-side F, out parallel to the axis
Beyond 2F: real, inverted, diminished — the camera
Between F and 2F: real, inverted, magnified — the projector
Inside F: virtual, upright, magnified on the object's side — the magnifying glass (Higher)
A real image can be caught on a screen; a virtual one cannot
notOnThisSpec: The construction of cameras and projectors as devices
The eye and the correction of sight defects

note.title: Ray diagrams for converging lenses: camera, projector and magnifying glass
note.subject: science

mustKnow: Scaffolding first: axis, lens, F and 2F on both sides, object
Ray 1: parallel to the axis, then through the far-side principal focus
Ray 2: straight through the optical centre, undeviated
Ray 3: through the near-side principal focus, then parallel to the axis
Every ray carries an arrowhead; the image goes where the rays cross
Beyond 2F: real, inverted, diminished (camera). Between F and 2F: real, inverted, magnified (projector)
Higher: inside F, virtual, upright, magnified on the object's side (magnifying glass)

notOnThisSpec: Magnification as a calculation (image height divided by object height)
The construction of a camera or a projector as devices
The eye, accommodation and the correction of sight defects

mustBeAbleTo: Draw the axis, the lens symbol, F and 2F on both sides, and the object, before any ray
Construct the three standard rays from the tip of the object, each with an arrowhead
Mark the image where the rays cross and read its distance and height off the grid
Describe an image as real or virtual, upright or inverted, magnified or diminished
Name the camera and the projector from where the object sits relative to F and 2F
Higher: construct the virtual image a converging lens gives when the object is inside F
Explain why a real image is inverted, and why a virtual one cannot be caught on a screen
Spot a ray that breaks its own rule on a printed construction
Work back from an object and its image to find F, as Higher papers ask (Summer 2025, Summer 2022)
sheet.howExamined: P2, 1 hour 15 minutes: 70 marks at Foundation, 80 at Higher, calculator allowed. A printed grid with the lens and object already on it, and a mark for each part of the construction: one per correctly drawn ray, one for the arrowheads, one for the image in the right place, then the three describing words. Summer 2024 Higher Q6(a) gave [5] for the magnifying-glass construction alone. Unit 7 Physics Booklet B has set the same content in writing, with the screen and a real image.
traps: Not being able to construct any correct ray at all (Summer 2025 P2 F Q3)
Drawing rays without a direction arrow (Summer 2025 P2 H Q7; the same slip on a mirror diagram, Summer 2024 P2 F Q2)
Not knowing where to label the focal point, so the ray rules have nothing to work from (Summer 2025 P2 H Q7)
Marking the image anywhere but where the rays actually cross (Summer 2025 P2 F Q3)
Drawing the image at the wrong distance or the wrong height from the constructed rays (Summer 2023 P2 H Q3)
Giving an image two properties that contradict each other, real and virtual or upright and inverted (Summer 2023 P2 F Q8; Summer 2023 P2 H Q3)
Not knowing the rules for the rays, so that no ray is drawn correctly (Summer 2023 P2 F Q8)
Not realising that a real image needs a screen to be seen, while a virtual one cannot be caught at all (Summer 2024 U7 Physics Booklet B Q2; Summer 2024 U7 Physics Booklet B Q4)
Getting the converging and diverging lenses the wrong way round (Summer 2024 P2 F Q2)
Drawing the magnifying-glass construction inaccurately, when its image belongs on the object's side (Summer 2024 P2 H Q6)

steps.working: Draw the axis and the lens, then mark F at 5 cm and 2F at 10 cm on both sides.
steps.decision: Two of the three ray rules are defined by F, so nothing can be drawn until the focal points are on the paper. Examiners have recorded them missing.

options: because the ray rules are defined by F
because F shows where the lens is
because F is where the object stands
whyMenu.explain: A ray arriving parallel goes through F, and a ray through F leaves parallel. Without F on the paper there are no rules to follow.

steps.working: Stand the object on the axis 15 cm to the left, 2 cm tall. It is beyond 2F.
steps.decision: Noting which region the object is in tells you what kind of image to expect before you draw a single ray.

steps.working: Draw ray 1 from the tip, parallel to the axis then through the far-side F; and ray 2 from the tip straight through the optical centre. Put an arrowhead on each.
steps.decision: Two rays are enough. The arrowheads are worth a mark on their own.

steps.working: The rays cross 7.5 cm beyond the lens, 1.0 cm below the axis.
steps.decision: Read both numbers off the grid rather than guessing, and draw the image as an arrow from the axis to that point.

steps.working: Three words, in order: real, inverted, diminished.
steps.decision: One word from each pair. A contradictory pair cancels, so never write two words from the same pair.

workedExamples.finalAnswer: The image is 7.5 cm from the lens on the far side, 1.0 cm tall, and it is real, inverted and diminished.

twin.stem: The same lens is used with the object 10 cm away, exactly at 2F. State the height of the image, in cm.

workedExamples.stem: The same 5 cm lens is held 3 cm above a page. Construct the ray diagram and describe the image.

figure.alt: A converging lens on a centimetre grid with an object 3 centimetres away, spreading rays and dashed backward extensions meeting at a large upright image on the object's side.

steps.working: 3 cm is less than the focal length of 5 cm, so the object is inside F.
steps.decision: Deciding which region the object is in is the step that tells you to expect a virtual image and to reach for dashed lines.

steps.working: Draw ray 1 (parallel, then through the far-side F) and ray 2 (straight through the optical centre). After the lens they are still spreading apart.
steps.decision: They never cross on the far side, so there is no real image to mark there.

steps.working: Extend both rays backwards as dashed lines. They cross 7.5 cm from the lens, on the same side as the object.
steps.decision: Dashed, because no light travels along those lines. That is what makes the image virtual.

options: because no light actually travels along them
because they are only rough guides
because they are behind the lens
whyMenu.explain: The dashed lines show where the light appears to come from. Nothing travels along them, which is exactly what virtual means.

steps.working: Draw the image there, upright, 5 cm tall against an object 2 cm tall.
steps.decision: Read the height off the grid. Bigger than the object, so magnified.

workedExamples.finalAnswer: The image is 7.5 cm from the lens on the same side as the page, 5 cm tall, and it is virtual, upright and magnified.

twin.stem: State whether the image a magnifying glass forms could be caught on a screen.

options.text: no, because it is virtual and no light arrives there
options.feedback: Correct: a virtual image cannot be caught.

options.text: yes, if the screen is held close enough to the lens
options.feedback: No position of the screen works: the light never reaches the place the image appears to be.

figure.alt: A converging lens on a centimetre grid with an object 7.5 centimetres away, between F and 2F, and a large inverted image far beyond the lens.

steps.working: The picture on the screen is much bigger than the slide, so the image must be magnified.
steps.decision: Start from what the device has to do, and work back to where the object goes.

steps.working: A converging lens only magnifies a real image when the object is between F and 2F.
steps.decision: Beyond 2F gives a diminished image; inside F gives a virtual one that no screen could catch.

steps.working: With the slide 7.5 cm from a 5 cm lens, the image lands 15 cm away and is 4 cm tall.
steps.decision: Read both off the grid; the image is further out than 2F, which is where a projector's screen goes.

steps.working: Three words: real, inverted, magnified.
steps.decision: Real is why a screen works at all, and inverted is why a projector slide is loaded upside down.

workedExamples.finalAnswer: The slide sits between F and 2F, and the image is real, inverted and magnified.

twin.stem: State where the object must be for a converging lens to give a real image the same size as the object.

accepted: at 2F
at twice the focal length
exactly at 2F

steps.working: Draw the axis and the lens, then mark F 6 cm and 2F 12 cm from the lens on both sides.
steps.decision: The ray rules are built on F, so it goes on the paper first, on both sides.

options: because two of the ray rules are defined by F
because F shows where the image will be
because the object must stand at F
whyMenu.explain: Parallel in means through F out, and through F in means parallel out. Without F on the paper those rays cannot be drawn.

steps.working: Stand the object 18 cm left of the lens, 3 cm tall: it is beyond 2F.
steps.decision: Its region says what to expect: beyond 2F gives the camera's image.

accepted: beyond 2F

any: more than twice the focal length
further than twice the focal length
greater than twice the focal length

steps.working: From the tip draw ray 1 parallel to the axis then through F, and ray 2 straight through the optical centre, each with an arrowhead.
steps.decision: Two rays fix the image; the arrowheads earn their own mark.

options.text: ray 1 parallel to the axis then through F on the far side, ray 2 straight through the centre, an arrow on each
options.feedback: Yes: the two rules, each ray with its arrow.

options.text: ray 1 parallel to the axis then through F on the object's side, ray 2 straight through the centre, an arrow on each
options.feedback: A parallel ray leaves through F on the far side; F on the object's side belongs to ray 3.

options.text: ray 1 parallel to the axis then through F on the far side, ray 2 bent at the centre, no arrows needed
options.feedback: The ray through the centre is not bent, and every ray needs its arrow: a mark goes on the arrows.

steps.working: The rays cross 9 cm beyond the lens, 1.5 cm below the axis: draw the image there.
steps.decision: Read both off the grid; the image goes only where the rays actually cross.

steps.working: Real, inverted, diminished.
steps.decision: One word from each pair: the rays really meet, the image points down, and it is half the object's height.

accepted: real, inverted, diminished

workedExamples.finalAnswer: The image is 9 cm beyond the lens and 1.5 cm tall: real, inverted and diminished.

twin.stem: The same lens is used with the object 12 cm away, at 2F. State how far from the lens the image forms, in cm.

steps.working: Mark F 6 cm and 2F 12 cm from the lens, on both sides.
steps.decision: F carries the ray rules; 2F tells you which case you have.

steps.working: The slide is 9 cm away: between F (6 cm) and 2F (12 cm).
steps.decision: That is the projector's region, so expect a large inverted image.

accepted: between F and 2F

any: between f and twice the focal length
between the focal length and twice the focal length
between one and two focal lengths
further than f but closer than 2f
further than f but nearer than 2f
further than f but less than 2f
more than f but less than 2f

options: because the region decides which image to expect
because the slide must always be at F
because the screen is always at 2F
whyMenu.explain: Beyond 2F, between F and 2F, and inside F each give their own image; placing the slide first tells you what the rays will show.

steps.working: From the slide's tip draw ray 1 parallel to the axis then through F, and ray 2 straight through the centre, with arrowheads.
steps.decision: The same two rules as every time, with their arrows.

options.text: ray 1 parallel to the axis then through F on the far side, ray 2 straight through the centre, an arrow on each
options.feedback: Yes: the two rules, each ray with its arrow.

options.text: ray 1 parallel to the axis then through F on the object's side, ray 2 straight through the centre, an arrow on each
options.feedback: A parallel ray leaves through F on the far side; F on the slide's side belongs to ray 3.

options.text: ray 1 parallel to the axis then through F on the far side, ray 2 bent at the centre, no arrows needed
options.feedback: The ray through the centre is not bent, and every ray needs its arrow: a mark goes on the arrows.

steps.working: The rays cross 18 cm beyond the lens, 4 cm below the axis.
steps.decision: Further out than 2F, which is where the screen must go.

steps.working: Real, inverted, magnified.
steps.decision: The rays really meet on the screen, the picture points down, and it is twice the slide's height.

accepted: real, inverted, magnified

workedExamples.finalAnswer: The image forms 18 cm beyond the lens and is 4 cm tall: real, inverted and magnified.

twin.stem: The slide is moved to 8 cm from the same lens, still further out than F. Does its image now form nearer to the lens or further from it?

options.text: further from the lens
options.feedback: Yes: as the object comes in towards F, the image moves out and grows.

options.text: nearer to the lens
options.feedback: As the object comes in towards F the image moves the other way, further out.

options.text: in the same place
options.feedback: Moving the object moves the image: here further from the lens.

figurePlain.alt: A lens of focal length 10 cm on a centimetre grid, F and 2F marked on both sides of it, and an object 2 cm tall standing 6 cm from the lens. No rays are drawn.

steps.working: Mark F 10 cm and 2F 20 cm from the lens on both sides; the stamp, at 6 cm, is inside F.
steps.decision: Inside F means expect a virtual image and dashed lines.

options: because inside F the rays leave the lens spreading
because inside F the image is always real
because inside F the rays meet at 2F
whyMenu.explain: With the object inside F the lens cannot bring the rays together, so they leave spreading and only seem to come from a point on the object's side.

steps.working: Draw ray 1 parallel to the axis then through F on the far side, and ray 2 straight through the centre, each with an arrowhead.
steps.decision: After the lens they spread apart, so they never cross on the far side.

options.text: ray 1 parallel then through F on the far side, ray 2 straight through the centre; after the lens they spread apart
options.feedback: Yes: inside F the two rays leave the lens spreading.

options.text: ray 1 parallel then through F on the far side, ray 2 straight through the centre; after the lens they cross on the far side
options.feedback: With the stamp inside F the rays leave the lens spreading, so they never cross on the far side.

options.text: ray 1 parallel then through F on the stamp's side, ray 2 straight through the centre; after the lens they spread apart
options.feedback: A parallel ray leaves through F on the far side; F on the stamp's side belongs to ray 3.

steps.working: Extend both rays backwards as dashed lines: they meet 15 cm from the lens, on the stamp's side.
steps.decision: Dashed, because no light travels along these lines; they only show where the rays seem to start.

steps.working: Draw the image there, dashed and upright, 5 cm tall.
steps.decision: Read its height off the grid: two and a half times the stamp's.

steps.working: Virtual, upright, magnified.
steps.decision: The light only seems to come from the image, it points the same way as the stamp, and it is larger.

accepted: virtual, upright, magnified

workedExamples.finalAnswer: The image is 15 cm from the lens on the stamp's side and 5 cm tall: virtual, upright and magnified.

twin.stem: The same magnifying glass is held 5 cm from the stamp. Which three words describe the image?

options.text: virtual, upright, magnified
options.feedback: Yes: 5 cm is still inside F (10 cm), so this is the magnifying glass's image.

options.text: real, inverted, magnified
options.feedback: That is the projector, with the object between F and 2F; at 5 cm the stamp is inside F.

options.text: real, inverted, diminished
options.feedback: That is the camera, with the object beyond 2F; at 5 cm the stamp is inside F.

steps.working: Draw a straight line from the object's tip to the image's tip.
steps.decision: It passes through the optical centre, which bends no ray: this is ray 2, and it needs no F.

options: because a ray through the optical centre goes straight on
because every ray goes straight through a lens
whyMenu.explain: Only the ray through the optical centre is not bent, so the straight line from tip to tip is that ray.

steps.working: From the object's tip draw a ray parallel to the axis as far as the lens.
steps.decision: This is ray 1: after the lens it must head through F.

options.text: a ray parallel to the axis as far as the lens
options.feedback: Yes: ray 1, which after the lens passes through F.

options.text: a ray through F on the object's side
options.feedback: F is not known yet, so a ray through it cannot be drawn; start with the parallel ray.

options.text: a ray from the image's tip back to the object
options.feedback: That is the line you already have, through the centre. The second ray starts parallel to the axis.

steps.working: Carry it on from the lens to the image's tip: it crosses the axis 2 cm beyond the lens.
steps.decision: A ray that arrived parallel always passes through F, so that crossing is F.

steps.working: The focal length is 2 cm.
steps.decision: Label the crossing F; the focal length is measured from the lens's centre.

twin.stem: An object 22 cm from a lens gives a sharp image 22 cm on the other side, the same size as the object. State the focal length, in cm.

items.stem: What does a converging lens do to rays that arrive parallel to its principal axis?
items.skill: Recalling the action of a converging lens

options.text: brings them together at the principal focus
options.feedback: Yes. That point is what every ray rule is built on.

options.text: spreads them apart
options.feedback: That is a diverging lens. A converging lens brings parallel rays together.

options.text: lets them carry straight on
options.feedback: Only the ray through the very centre carries straight on.

items.stem: Which two points does the focal length of a converging lens run between?
items.skill: Recalling the definition of focal length

options.text: the optical centre and the principal focus
options.feedback: Yes, and both of those get marked on every ray diagram.

options.text: the lens and the object
options.feedback: That is the object distance, and it changes as the object moves.

options.text: the two principal focuses
options.feedback: That distance is twice the focal length.

items.stem: On a diagram, what does a dashed line usually mean?

options.text: that no light actually travels along it
options.feedback: Yes. The same convention is used for a virtual image in a mirror.

options.text: that the light is very faint there
options.feedback: Dashed does not mean dim; it means no light goes that way at all.

options.text: that the line is only a rough guess
options.feedback: Construction lines are drawn just as carefully as the rays.

items.stem: What does virtual mean when it describes an image?
items.skill: Recalling real and virtual from reflection

options.text: the light only appears to come from there
options.feedback: Yes, which is why a screen catches nothing.

options.text: the image is not really visible
options.feedback: A virtual image is perfectly visible; it just cannot be caught on a screen.

options.text: the image is smaller than the object
options.feedback: Size is a separate judgement from real or virtual.

items.stem: A ray leaves the tip of the object parallel to the principal axis. What does it do at the lens?

options.text: it refracts through the principal focus on the far side
options.feedback: Yes: parallel in, through F out.

options.text: it refracts through the principal focus on the near side
options.feedback: The near-side F is where ray 3 comes from, not where ray 1 goes.

options.text: it carries straight on
options.feedback: Only the ray through the optical centre carries straight on.

options.text: it reflects back the way it came
options.feedback: A lens refracts light through itself; it does not send it back.

items.stem: What must every ray on a lens diagram carry?

options.text: an arrowhead showing which way the light travels
options.feedback: Yes, and it is worth a mark of its own.

options.text: a label naming the colour of the light
options.feedback: Colour is not part of this construction, and it earns nothing.

options.text: the angle it makes with the lens, in degrees
options.feedback: No angles are measured on a lens diagram; the rules do the work.

options.text: nothing: a plain straight line is enough
options.feedback: A line without an arrow does not say which way the light went, and the construction marks are lost.

items.stem: An object sits beyond 2F from a converging lens. Which three words describe the image?

options.text: real, inverted, diminished
options.feedback: Yes. That is the camera case.

options.text: real, inverted, magnified
options.feedback: That is the projector case, with the object between F and 2F.

options.text: virtual, upright, magnified
options.feedback: That is the magnifying-glass case, with the object inside F.

options.text: real, upright, diminished
options.feedback: A real image from a converging lens is always inverted, so real and upright cannot go together here.

items.stem: Where must the object be for a converging lens to give a virtual image?
items.skill: The condition for a virtual image

options.text: closer to the lens than the principal focus
options.feedback: Yes. Inside F the rays leave still spreading.

options.text: exactly at 2F
options.feedback: At 2F the image is real, inverted and the same size as the object.

options.text: beyond 2F
options.feedback: Beyond 2F the image is real, inverted and diminished.

options.text: a converging lens never gives a virtual image
options.feedback: It does, whenever the object is inside F. That is how a magnifying glass works.

items.stem: Why can the image formed by a magnifying glass not be caught on a screen?

options.text: no light actually arrives where the image appears to be
options.feedback: Yes. That is exactly what virtual means.

options.text: the image is too bright for a screen
options.feedback: Brightness is not the issue; no light reaches that point at all.

options.text: the image is too big to fit on a screen
options.feedback: Size is not the issue either. A virtual image cannot be caught however small it is.

options.text: the image is the wrong way up for a screen
options.feedback: It is upright, and in any case a screen would show an inverted image perfectly well.

items.stem: A student writes that the image is real and virtual, inverted and magnified. What does the examiner do?

options.text: cancels the real-or-virtual mark and credits the other two
options.feedback: Yes. Contradictory ticks cancel, so choose one word from each pair.

options.text: gives all three marks, since the right word is there
options.feedback: A correct answer written next to a wrong one earns nothing for that pair: that is the listing rule.

options.text: gives no marks at all for the whole answer
options.feedback: Only the contradicted pair is lost; the other two words still count.

options.text: credits whichever word was written first
options.feedback: The scheme does not pick a favourite; the pair simply cancels.

items.stem: In a projector, where does the slide sit?
items.skill: Naming the device from the object position

options.text: between F and 2F
options.feedback: Yes, which is why the picture on the screen is bigger than the slide.

options.text: beyond 2F
options.feedback: That would give a picture smaller than the slide, which is a camera, not a projector.

options.text: closer than F
options.feedback: That gives a virtual image, and no screen could show it.

options.text: exactly at F
options.feedback: At F the rays leave parallel and no image forms at any finite distance.

parts.stem:
A ray leaves the tip of the object travelling parallel to the principal axis.
State the path it takes after the lens.

options.text: it refracts through the principal focus on the far side of the lens
options.feedback: Correct. Parallel in, through F out.

options.text: it refracts through the principal focus on the near side of the lens
options.feedback: That is the wrong side. The near-side F is where ray 3 comes from, not where ray 1 goes.

options.text: it carries straight on, parallel to the axis
options.feedback: Only the ray through the optical centre carries straight on.

scheme.for: through the principal focus on the far side

parts.workedSolution: It refracts at the lens and passes through the principal focus on the far side. That is ray 1: parallel in, through F out.

hints: Think about the shape of the lens right at its middle.
parts.stem:
A second ray leaves the tip of the object and passes through the optical centre of the lens.
State the path it takes after the lens.

options.text: it carries straight on, undeviated
options.feedback: Correct. At the centre the two faces are parallel, so the ray comes out going the way it went in.

options.text: it refracts through the principal focus
options.feedback: That is the rule for the ray that arrived parallel to the axis.

options.text: it leaves parallel to the axis
options.feedback: That is the rule for the ray that came in through the near-side F.

parts.workedSolution: It carries straight on, undeviated. At the optical centre the two faces of the lens are parallel, so the ray leaves in the direction it arrived.

hints: A line without an arrow does not say which way the light went.
Two rays are enough to find the image, so what is the third for?

commonErrors.feedback: Labels are useful, but the mark here is for the arrowhead on each ray: it is what shows the direction the light travelled.

parts.stem: State what every ray you draw must carry, and why the third ray is worth drawing at all.

accepted: Every ray must carry an arrowhead to show which way the light travels, and the third ray is a check that the first two were drawn correctly.
An arrow on each ray shows the direction of the light, and the third ray should land on the same point, so it checks the other two.

scheme.for: an arrow (arrowhead) showing the direction the light travels
scheme.examinerNote: Summer 2024 and Summer 2025 both recorded rays drawn without direction arrows.

scheme.for: the third ray should meet the same point, so it checks the construction

parts.workedSolution: Every ray must carry an arrowhead showing which way the light travels; marks are given for the construction, and a ray without an arrow is only a line. The third ray should land on the same crossing point as the first two, so drawing it checks the work.

commonErrors.feedback: The rays cannot be drawn until F is marked, because two of the three rules are defined by it. Axis, lens, F and 2F on both sides, object, then the rays.

parts.stem:
The six steps of constructing a converging-lens ray diagram are listed in the wrong order.
Put them in the order they should be carried out.

expectedOrder: Draw the principal axis as a horizontal line across the page.
Draw the lens as a vertical line through the axis, with an arrowhead at each end.
Mark F and 2F on the axis on both sides of the lens, equally spaced.
Draw the object as an upright arrow standing on the axis.
Draw two rays from the tip of the object, each with an arrowhead.
Mark the image as an arrow where the two rays cross.

scheme.for: the axis and the lens are drawn first
F and 2F are marked on both sides before any ray
scheme.examinerNote: Summer 2025 P2 Higher: many candidates were unsure where to label the focal point, and two of the three ray rules are defined by F.

scheme.for: the rays are drawn from the tip of the object, and the image is marked where they cross

parts.workedSolution: 1. Draw the principal axis as a horizontal line across the page. 2. Draw the lens as a vertical line through the axis, with an arrowhead at each end. 3. Mark F and 2F on the axis on both sides of the lens, equally spaced. 4. Draw the object as an upright arrow standing on the axis. 5. Draw two rays from the tip of the object, each with an arrowhead. 6. Mark the image as an arrow where the two rays cross.

hints: Read across from where the rays cross to the axis, then count the squares back to the lens.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the principal focus. The image only sits at F when the object is so far away that its rays arrive parallel; here it is 7.5 cm out.
That is the object distance. The image distance is read on the other side of the lens, where the rays cross.

parts.stem:
The grid is marked in centimetres. The lens has a focal length of 5 cm and the object is 15 cm from it and 2 cm tall.
Use the diagram to state how far the image is from the lens, in cm.

scheme.examinerNote: Summer 2023 P2 Higher: marks went on the image not being drawn at the right distance from the optical centre.

parts.workedSolution: The rays cross 7.5 cm beyond the lens, which is between F (5 cm) and 2F (10 cm).

hints: Count the squares from the axis to the tip of the image arrow.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the height of the object. The image is a different size, which is the whole point of the three describing words.
That is the height the image reaches when the object sits between F and 2F. This object is further out than 2F, so the image is smaller than the object.

parts.stem: Use the diagram to state the height of the image, in cm.
parts.workedSolution: The image arrow reaches 1.0 cm below the axis, against an object 2 cm tall.

hints: Ask whether a screen held there would catch a picture.
parts.stem: State whether the image is real or virtual.

options.text: real
options.feedback: Correct: the rays really cross there, so the image could be caught on a screen.

options.text: virtual
options.feedback: The rays really do cross on the far side, so light arrives at the image and it is real.

parts.workedSolution: Real. The rays actually cross at the image, so light arrives there and a screen would show a picture.

hints: Look at which way the image arrow points on your construction.
parts.stem: State whether the image is upright or inverted.

options.text: upright
options.feedback: The rays from the top of the object end up below the axis, so the image points the other way.

options.text: inverted
options.feedback: Correct: the rays cross at the lens, so the top of the object maps below the axis.

parts.workedSolution: Inverted. The rays from the tip of the object cross over at the lens, so the tip of the image ends up below the axis.

hints: Compare the height of the image with the height of the object.
parts.stem: State whether the image is magnified or diminished.

options.text: magnified
options.feedback: The image is 1.0 cm tall against an object 2 cm tall, so it is smaller.

options.text: diminished
options.feedback: Correct: 1.0 cm against an object 2 cm tall.

scheme.examinerNote: Contradictory pairs cancel each other out: real with virtual, upright with inverted.

parts.workedSolution: The image is 1.0 cm tall and the object is 2 cm tall, so the image is diminished.

parts.stem: Name the everyday device that uses a converging lens with the object in this position.

options.text: a projector
options.feedback: Correct: the slide sits between F and 2F so the picture on the screen is bigger than the slide.

options.text: a camera
options.feedback: In a camera the object is beyond 2F, so the image is smaller than the object and fits on the sensor.

options.text: a magnifying glass
options.feedback: A magnifying glass has the object closer than F, which gives a virtual, upright image.

parts.workedSolution: A projector. The slide or film sits between F and 2F, so the image on the screen is real, inverted and magnified — which is why a projector slide is loaded upside down.

parts.stem: State whether the image is real or virtual.

options.text: real
options.feedback: The rays leave the lens still spreading and never cross, so nothing arrives where the image appears to be.

options.text: virtual
options.feedback: Correct: the rays only appear to come from there, so a screen would catch nothing.

options.text: upright

options.text: inverted

figures.alt: A converging lens on a centimetre grid with an object 15 centimetres away and one ray drawn from the top of the object, travelling parallel to the axis as far as the lens.

hints: The image tip is below the axis, because the image is inverted.
The refracted ray leaves the lens at a height of 2 cm and crosses the axis at the principal focus.

commonErrors.feedback: The image is inverted, so its tip belongs below the axis at (7.5, −1.0). Drawing it above the axis makes it upright, which contradicts a real image from an object beyond 2F.

parts.stem:
The grid is marked in centimetres, with the lens at 0 and distances to the right of it positive. The object stands 15 cm to the left of the lens and is 2 cm tall, so its tip is at (−15, 2).
Place the tip of the object and the tip of the image, then lay the refracted ray that leaves the lens and passes through the principal focus.

scheme.for: the tip of the object placed correctly
the tip of the image placed where the rays cross, below the axis
the refracted ray laid from the lens through the principal focus to the image tip
scheme.examinerNote: Summer 2025 P2 Higher: marks went on rays drawn without a direction arrow, and on the image not being placed where the rays actually cross.

parts.workedSolution: The object tip is at (−15, 2). The refracted ray leaves the lens at (0, 2), crosses the axis at the principal focus (5, 0) and reaches the image tip at (7.5, −1.0).

figures.alt: Two converging lenses side by side, each on its own principal axis with its principal focus F marked, an object arrow and the image of it, and a screen standing exactly at the image. On the left the object is well beyond F and a small inverted image forms on the far side of the lens. On the right the object is between F and the lens and a larger upright image, drawn dashed, sits on the same side as the object.

hints: Which image has light actually arriving at it?
parts.stem: State which of the two images in the diagram could be caught on a screen.

options.text: the real image, on the left
options.feedback: Correct. Light really arrives there, so a screen shows a picture.

options.text: the virtual image, on the right
options.feedback: No light reaches where a virtual image appears to be, so a screen there stays blank.

options.text: both of them
options.feedback: Only one of them has light arriving at it. The virtual one is where the rays merely appear to come from.

parts.workedSolution: The real image. Light really converges there, so a screen placed at that point shows a picture; a virtual image has no light arriving at it.

hints: Name the kind of image first.
Then say what is not happening at that point.

commonErrors.feedback: A real image can be caught on a screen. The one a magnifying glass forms cannot, which is what makes it virtual.

parts.stem: Explain why a screen held where the magnifying glass appears to form its image shows nothing. [2]

accepted: The image is virtual, so no light actually reaches that place: the rays only appear to come from there.
Because the rays leave the lens still spreading and never cross, so nothing arrives at the point they seem to come from.

scheme.for: the image is virtual / the rays only appear to come from there
no light actually arrives at that point

parts.workedSolution: The image is virtual: the rays leave the lens still spreading and never actually cross, so no light arrives at the point they appear to come from. A screen there has nothing landing on it.

figures.alt: Two converging lenses side by side, each on its own principal axis with its principal focus F marked, an object arrow and the image of it, and a screen standing exactly at the image. On the left the object is well beyond F and a small inverted image forms on the far side of the lens. On the right the object is between F and the lens and a larger upright image, drawn dashed, sits on the same side as the object.

hints: Which image has light actually arriving at it?
parts.stem: State which of the two images in the diagram could be caught on a screen.

options.text: the real image, on the left
options.feedback: Correct. Light really arrives there, so a screen shows a picture.

options.text: the virtual image, on the right
options.feedback: No light reaches where a virtual image appears to be, so a screen there stays blank.

options.text: both of them
options.feedback: Only one of them has light arriving at it. The virtual one is where the rays merely appear to come from.

parts.workedSolution: The real image. Light really converges there, so a screen placed at that point shows a picture; a virtual image has no light arriving at it.

hints: Name the kind of image first.
Then say what is not happening at that point.

commonErrors.feedback: A real image can be caught on a screen. The one a magnifying glass forms cannot, which is what makes it virtual.

parts.stem: Explain why a screen held where the magnifying glass appears to form its image shows nothing. [2]

accepted: The image is virtual, so no light actually reaches that place: the rays only appear to come from there.
Because the rays leave the lens still spreading and never cross, so nothing arrives at the point they seem to come from.

scheme.for: the image is virtual / the rays only appear to come from there
no light actually arrives at that point

parts.workedSolution: The image is virtual: the rays leave the lens still spreading and never actually cross, so no light arrives at the point they appear to come from. A screen there has nothing landing on it.

context.setting: A camera and a projector, both built round a converging lens

figures.alt: Three converging-lens diagrams stacked on the same scale with the object at three different distances, each with a second short line marking where the image sits.

hints: Say where the object sits, using F and 2F.
Then give the three describing words, or at least the size one.

commonErrors.feedback: Between F and 2F is the projector's arrangement, which magnifies. A camera needs the object beyond 2F so the picture is small enough for the sensor.

parts.stem:
A camera and a projector both use a converging lens, but the object is put in a different place in each.
Explain where the object goes in a camera, and what that gives. [2]

accepted: In a camera the object is beyond 2F, so the image is real, inverted and diminished, small enough to fit on the sensor.
The object is further from the lens than 2F, which gives a real inverted image smaller than the object.

scheme.for: so the image is real, inverted and diminished

parts.workedSolution: In a camera the object is beyond 2F, so the image is real, inverted and diminished — small enough to land on the sensor inside the camera.

hints: A projector needs a picture bigger than the slide.
parts.stem: Explain where the slide goes in a projector, and what that gives. [2]

accepted: In a projector the slide is between F and 2F, so the image is real, inverted and magnified, big enough for a screen.
The slide sits between the principal focus and 2F, which gives a real inverted image larger than the slide.

scheme.for: the slide is between F and 2F
so the image is real, inverted and magnified

parts.workedSolution: In a projector the slide is between F and 2F, so the image is real, inverted and magnified — which is why the slide is loaded upside down.

hints: Two of the three describing words match.
parts.stem: State the one thing that is the same about both images.

accepted: both images are real and inverted
they are both real and inverted
both are inverted and real

parts.workedSolution: Both images are real and inverted. Only the size is different, because only the object distance is different.

context.setting: A camera and a projector, both built round a converging lens

Then give the three describing words, or at least the size one.

commonErrors.feedback: Between F and 2F is the projector's arrangement, which magnifies. A camera needs the object beyond 2F so the picture is small enough for the sensor.

A camera and a projector both use a converging lens, but the object is put in a different place in each.

accepted: In a camera the object is beyond 2F, so the image is real, inverted and diminished, small enough to fit on the sensor.
The object is further from the lens than 2F, which gives a real inverted image smaller than the object.

scheme.for: so the image is real, inverted and diminished

hints: A projector needs a picture bigger than the slide.

accepted: In a projector the slide is between F and 2F, so the image is real, inverted and magnified, big enough for a screen.
The slide sits between the principal focus and 2F, which gives a real inverted image larger than the slide.

between the focal length and twice the focal length

so the image is real, inverted and magnified

accepted: both images are real and inverted
they are both real, and both inverted

parts.stem:
A student has a converging lens of known focal length, a lit object and a screen on an optical bench. They want to predict, before they try it, what the image will look like when the object is placed a long way beyond 2F.
Describe how to construct the ray diagram that answers this, and describe the image it predicts. [6]
This question also assesses the quality of your written communication, including your use of specialist scientific terms.

bands.descriptor: Five or six of the indicative points, described in detail, with specialist terms used widely and accurately; the ideas are ordered very clearly and follow on from one another; spelling, punctuation and grammar make the meaning clear throughout.

Three or four of the indicative points; some specialist vocabulary; the ideas are ordered reasonably well and mostly follow on; spelling, punctuation and grammar are competent enough for the meaning to be clear.
One or two of the indicative points; little specialist vocabulary; the organisation may lack clarity; spelling, punctuation and grammar may leave the intended meaning unclear.

indicativeContent.point: draw the principal axis and the lens as a vertical line with arrowheads
mark F and 2F on the axis on both sides of the lens
draw the object as an upright arrow standing on the axis beyond 2F
draw a ray from the tip parallel to the axis, refracting through the far-side F
draw a ray from the tip straight through the optical centre, undeviated
put an arrowhead on every ray to show the direction of the light
mark the image where the rays cross, between F and 2F on the far side
describe the image as real, inverted and diminished

scheme.for: banded: count the indicative points present, then place within the band on the quality of written communication — Band A [5]-[6] five or six points, Band B [3]-[4] three or four, Band C [1]-[2] one or two, [0] response not worthy of credit
scheme.examinerNote: A point contradicted elsewhere in the answer is not counted: real and virtual together, or upright and inverted together, cancel. The specialist words the scheme wants are principal axis, principal focus, optical centre, real, inverted and diminished.

parts.workedSolution: Draw the principal axis as a horizontal line and the lens as a vertical line through it with an arrowhead at each end. Mark F and 2F on the axis on both sides of the lens, equally spaced. Draw the object as an upright arrow standing on the axis, further from the lens than 2F. From the tip of the object draw one ray parallel to the axis, which refracts at the lens and passes through the principal focus on the far side; draw a second ray from the tip straight through the optical centre, undeviated. Put an arrowhead on each ray to show which way the light travels. The two rays cross between F and 2F on the far side, and the image is drawn there as an arrow below the axis. The image is real, inverted and diminished.

parts.stem:

options.text: further from the lens than 2F

options.text: between F and 2F

findTheMistake.stem: A student is listing the rules they will use to construct a converging-lens ray diagram.
studentWorking: Ray 1 leaves the tip parallel to the axis and refracts through the principal focus on the far side.
Ray 2 leaves the tip and passes through the optical centre, where it is refracted downwards.
The image is marked where the two rays cross.
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Line 2 bends the ray at the optical centre. At the very middle the two faces of the lens are parallel, so that ray carries straight on, undeviated.
correction: Ray 1 leaves the tip parallel to the axis and refracts through the principal focus on the far side.
Ray 2 leaves the tip and passes straight through the optical centre, undeviated.
The image is marked where the two rays cross.
findTheMistake.feedback: Lines 1 and 3 are exactly right and would earn their marks. Bending the centre ray moves the crossing point, so the image ends up in the wrong place.

findTheMistake.stem: A student is describing their construction for an object at 2F from a lens of focal length 5 cm.
studentWorking: The object is at 2F, which is 10 cm from the lens.
I drew the two rays, and I marked the image at F, 5 cm from the lens.
The image is real and inverted.
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Line 2 puts the image at F out of habit. The image goes where the rays actually cross, and for an object at 2F that is 10 cm on the other side, not 5 cm.
correction: The object is at 2F, which is 10 cm from the lens.
I drew the two rays, and they crossed 10 cm from the lens, at 2F on the other side.
The image is real and inverted, and the same size as the object.
findTheMistake.feedback: Line 1 and the two describing words in line 3 are right. The image only sits at F when the object is so far away that its rays arrive parallel.

findTheMistake.stem: A student is describing the image a camera lens forms.
studentWorking: The object is beyond 2F, so the rays cross between F and 2F on the other side.
The image can be caught on the sensor, so it is real, and it is virtual as well because you cannot see it directly.
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Line 2 claims the image is both real and virtual. Those two words are a pair: an image is one or the other, and writing both cancels the mark.
correction: The object is beyond 2F, so the rays cross between F and 2F on the other side.
The image can be caught on the sensor, so it is real.
findTheMistake.feedback: Line 1 and line 3 are right and earn their marks. Choose one word from each of the three pairs and never write both.

prompts.prompt: What do you draw before any ray on a converging-lens diagram?
prompts.answer: The principal axis, the lens as a vertical line with arrowheads, F and 2F on both sides, and the object as an upright arrow on the axis.

prompts.prompt: What goes on the paper before any ray is drawn?
prompts.answer: The axis, the lens, F and 2F on both sides, and the object.

prompts.prompt: State the three standard rays for a converging lens.
prompts.answer: A ray parallel to the axis that refracts through the far-side principal focus; a ray straight through the optical centre, undeviated; and a ray through the near-side principal focus that leaves parallel to the axis.

prompts.prompt: State the three standard rays for a converging lens.
prompts.answer: Parallel then through F; straight through the centre; through the near F then parallel. An arrow on each.

prompts.prompt: What must every ray carry, and why does it matter?
prompts.answer: An arrowhead showing which way the light travels, because the marks are for the construction and a ray without an arrow is only a line.

prompts.prompt: Object beyond 2F: which three words describe the image, and which device is it?
prompts.answer: Real, inverted and diminished, which is the camera.

prompts.prompt: Object between F and 2F: which three words describe the image, and which device is it?
prompts.answer: Real, inverted and magnified, which is the projector.

prompts.prompt: Object closer to the lens than F: which three words describe the image, and which device is it?
prompts.answer: Virtual, upright and magnified, which is the magnifying glass.

prompts.prompt: Why is the real image from a converging lens inverted?
prompts.answer: Because the rays from the top of the object cross over at the lens and arrive below the axis.

prompts.prompt: How do you tell a real image from a virtual one in one test?
prompts.answer: Hold a screen where the image should be: a real image forms a picture on it, and a virtual image leaves it blank, because no light actually arrives there.

prompts.prompt: How does a screen tell a real image from a virtual one?
prompts.answer: A real image forms a picture on it; a virtual one leaves it blank.

prompts.prompt: Why are the construction lines for a magnifying-glass image drawn dashed?
prompts.answer: Because no light travels along them: they show where the rays only appear to come from, which is what makes the image virtual.

prompts.prompt: A magnifying glass held up to a distant tree shows it upside down and small. Explain why.
prompts.answer: The tree is beyond 2F, and an object beyond 2F gives a real, inverted, diminished image. What changes between the two uses of the lens is the object distance, not the lens.

findings.asked: Identify a lens, complete a ray diagram, describe the image.
findings.wentWrong: The lens was recognised, but the ray diagram was poorly done - many did not know the rules; image descriptions contradicted themselves (real and virtual, upright and inverted).
findings.rule: Two rules: parallel ray passes through F; ray through the centre goes straight on. Choose one word from each pair.

findings.asked: The same diagram at Higher, to scale.
findings.wentWrong: The rules were known, but marks went on the image not being 6 cm from the optical centre and 2 cm tall, and on contradictory descriptions again.
findings.rule: The image is where the rays cross - measure its position and size from the grid.

findings.asked: A mirror ray diagram, then converging and diverging lenses and a scaffolded lens diagram.
findings.wentWrong: Arrows were left off rays; a significant minority swapped converging and diverging; the scaffolding made the lens diagram go much better than in earlier series.
findings.rule: Every ray has an arrow; converging lens is fatter in the middle and brings rays together.

findings.asked: Finding a converging lens's focal length, then drawing a ray diagram.
findings.wentWrong: Most got at least one of the three steps for the focal length; a significant minority could not draw any correct ray, and only a small minority placed the image correctly.
findings.rule: Distant object, screen, move until sharp, measure lens to screen; then draw the two standard rays.

findings.asked: Draw the ray diagram and describe the image.
findings.wentWrong: Well drawn by many, but marks went on missing direction arrows and on not knowing where to label the focal point; almost everyone knew the image was real.
findings.rule: Label F on the axis at the focal length on both sides; arrows on every ray.

findings.asked: Complete a definition of focal length, then say how the real image would be viewed.
findings.wentWrong: The ray diagram was attempted well but the definition's key term was missing; only a small minority realised a screen is needed to see a real image, although many knew it was inverted.
findings.rule: A real image forms where rays actually meet and can be caught on a screen; a virtual image cannot.

insight.ruleToRemember: Two rays fix the image: the ray parallel to the axis refracts through F, the ray through the optical centre is undeviated; draw arrows on both, label F on both sides, and draw the image where they cross. Object beyond F: real, inverted, on a screen (camera, projector). Object inside F: virtual, upright, magnified (magnifying glass). Read position and size off the grid.
insight.aStarSignal: Drawing to scale, stating the image's position and height from the diagram, and choosing consistent words for nature, orientation and size.
